Online LLM watermark detection via e-processes

Weijie Su ††thanks: Department of Statistics and Data Science, University of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia, USA. E-mail: suw@wharton.upenn.edu    Ruodu Wang ††thanks: Department of Statistics and Actuarial Science, University of Waterloo, Waterloo, Ontario, Canada. E-mail: wang@uwaterloo.ca    Zinan Zhao ††thanks: Center for Data Science and School of Mathematical Sciences, Zhejiang University, Hangzhou, China. E-mail: znzh@zju.edu.cn
August 24, 2026
Abstract

Watermarking for large language models (LLMs) has emerged as an effective tool for distinguishing AI-generated text from human-written content. Statistically, watermark schemes induce dependence between generated tokens and a pseudo-random sequence, reducing watermark detection to a hypothesis testing problem on independence. We develop a unified framework for LLM watermark detection based on e-processes, providing anytime-valid guarantees for online testing. We propose various methods to construct empirically adaptive e-processes that can enhance the detection power. In addition, theoretical results are established to characterize the power properties of the proposed procedures. Some experiments demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves competitive performance compared to existing watermark detection methods.


Keywords: Watermark detection, anytime validity, e-processes, independence test

††footnotetext: Authors are listed in alphabetical order.

1 Introduction

The recent advent of powerful Large Language Models (LLMs) has fundamentally transformed natural language generation. State-of-the-art LLMs such as GPT-4 (Achiam et al.,, 2024) and LLaMA (Grattafiori et al.,, 2024) demonstrate remarkable capabilities in producing human-like text. While these advances unlock substantial societal and economic benefits, they also raise significant ethical and security concerns. The increasing difficulty in distinguishing AI-generated text from human-written content facilitates its misuse for malicious purposes, including generation of misinformation (Zellers et al.,, 2019; Starbird,, 2019; Weidinger et al.,, 2021), academic plagiarism (Stokel-Walker,, 2022; Milano et al.,, 2023), and automated fraudulent content generation (Shumailov et al.,, 2023; Das et al.,, 2024). Such misuse may seriously erode trust in digital ecosystems. To mitigate these problems, there is a pressing need for effective mechanisms to make AI-generated text distinguishable while preserving the quality and usability of language models.

Watermarking has emerged as a promising approach to address this challenge (Fernandez et al.,, 2023; Kuditipudi et al.,, 2024; Hu et al.,, 2024). In watermark schemes for LLMs, a subtle algorithmic signal is embedded into the text generation process, enabling post-hoc verification of AI authorship without significantly degrading text quality. From a statistical perspective, watermark schemes modify the sampling procedure of the language model.

Concretely, let 𝒲\mathcal{W} denote the vocabulary of tokens. Given a sequence of previous tokens (w1,…,wt−1)(w_{1},\ldots,w_{t-1}), an unwatermarked language model computes a next-token prediction (NTP) distribution 𝐏t\mathbf{P}_{t} and samples wtw_{t} from 𝐏t\mathbf{P}_{t}. In contrast, a watermarked model generates wtw_{t} according to both 𝐏t\mathbf{P}_{t} and a pseudo-random variable (or vector) ζt\zeta_{t}. In practice, the pseudo-random sequence can be reconstructed using the generated text together with shared secret information, referred to as the watermark key. A formal description of this mechanism is deferred to Section 3. Crucially, the watermark mechanism induces statistical dependence between wtw_{t} and ζt\zeta_{t}. In unwatermarked text generation, wtw_{t} is independent of ζt\zeta_{t}, whereas in watermarked generation, this independence is deliberately violated. Therefore, watermark detection can be formulated as a hypothesis testing problem on the dependence structure between the observed tokens and the pseudo-random variables (Aaronson,, 2023; Li et al., 2025b, ; Li et al., 2025c, ; Piet et al.,, 2025).

Despite substantial progress, existing watermark detection methods still face several challenges. First, most procedures are designed for fixed-sample testing and lack rigorous guarantees under optional stopping, which is particularly problematic in sequential or streaming settings. Second, statistical power may deteriorate when the NTP distribution becomes highly concentrated (i.e., nearly degenerate), a phenomenon that may occur in long text generation. Third, theoretical characterizations of testing power remain limited in general watermark detection frameworks.

To address these issues, we develop a unified framework for watermark detection based on e-values and e-processes, which are recently developed tools for online testing with useful features (Grünwald et al.,, 2024; Vovk and Wang,, 2021; Wang and Ramdas,, 2022; Ramdas et al.,, 2023); see Ramdas and Wang, (2025) for background and a comprehensive treatment of the topic. Our framework reformulates watermark detection as sequential hypothesis testing of independence and constructs e-processes tailored to the watermark-induced structure, with a special focus on the popular Gumbel-max watermark (Aaronson,, 2023). The proposed approach enjoys the following key advantages:

  1. 1.

    The proposed testing procedures control Type I error under arbitrary stopping times, making them suitable for real-time and streaming detection scenarios.

  2. 2.

    By using adaptive weights and the online Grenander algorithm (Hore et al.,, 2026) to construct calibrators, the proposed e-processes are flexible and have good performance. In some situations, they can even have better performance than the existing methods that do not have sequential validity.

  3. 3.

    We establish asymptotic power-one results under specific conditions, providing formal justification for the effectiveness of the proposed procedures.

Together, these contributions provide a principled and theoretically grounded approach to watermark detection. Our framework unifies existing ideas under the lens of e-processes, clarifies the statistical structure of watermark detection, and offers both finite-sample guarantees and asymptotic efficiency. Empirical studies further demonstrate the practical advantages of the proposed methods.

2 Preliminaries

2.1 Setting

Suppose that there are K≥2K\geq 2 tokens in the vocabulary 𝒲\mathcal{W} of the LLM. We write [n]={1,…,n}[n]=\{1,\dots,n\} for n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N} and 𝒲=[K]\mathcal{W}=[K].

The statistical task is to test whether a given text with TT tokens is generated by human, represented by a probability ℙ\mathbb{P}, or an LLM, represented by a probability ℚ\mathbb{Q}. As usual in online testing, the value of TT does not need to be known a priori, and it can be infinite. We set 𝕋=[T]\mathbb{T}=[T] if T<∞T<\infty and 𝕋=ℕ\mathbb{T}=\mathbb{N} if T=∞T=\infty. Moreover, 𝕋0=𝕋∪{0}\mathbb{T}_{0}=\mathbb{T}\cup\{0\}.

Let ΔK\Delta_{K} be the standard simplex in ℝK\mathbb{R}^{K}. For δ>0\delta>0, let ΔKδ\Delta^{\delta}_{K} be the set of vectors 𝐏\mathbf{P} in ΔK\Delta_{K} such that max⁡(𝐏)≤1−δ\max(\mathbf{P})\leq 1-\delta. Implicitly we require 1−δ≥1/K1-\delta\geq 1/K; otherwise ΔKδ\Delta^{\delta}_{K} is empty, but this is not a problem as we are mainly interested in the case where δ\delta is close to 00. Let ΔK∘=⋃δ>0ΔKδ\Delta^{\circ}_{K}=\bigcup_{\delta>0}\Delta^{\delta}_{K}, which is the set of vectors in ΔK\Delta_{K} with at least two positive components. If 𝐏\mathbf{P} only has one positive component, then we say that it is degenerate.

For the tt-th token, the NTP is represented by a vector of probability 𝐏t=(Pt,w)w∈𝒲\mathbf{P}_{t}=(P_{t,w})_{w\in\mathcal{W}} in ΔK\Delta_{K}. We use a filtration ℱ=(ℱt)t∈𝕋0\mathcal{F}=(\mathcal{F}_{t})_{t\in\mathbb{T}_{0}} to represent the information available before generating each token, and ℙt\mathbb{P}_{t} and ℚt\mathbb{Q}_{t} are the conditional probability given ℱt−1\mathcal{F}_{t-1}. We assume that the NTP vector 𝐏t\mathbf{P}_{t} is ℱt−1\mathcal{F}_{t-1}-measurable for t∈𝕋t\in\mathbb{T}. The vector 𝐏t\mathbf{P}_{t} governs how the token WtW_{t} is generated, that is,

ℙt​(Wt=w)=ℚt​(Wt=w)=Pt,w​ for w∈𝒲.\mathbb{P}_{t}(W_{t}=w)=\mathbb{Q}_{t}(W_{t}=w)=P_{t,w}\mbox{ for $w\in\mathcal{W}$.}

For 𝐏∈ΔK\mathbf{P}\in\Delta_{K}, we write 𝐏=(P1,…,PK)\mathbf{P}=(P_{1},\dots,P_{K}), and the entropy of 𝐏∈ΔK\mathbf{P}\in\Delta_{K} is defined as

Ent(𝐏)=−∑w∈𝒲PwlogPw.\mathrm{Ent}(\mathbf{P})=-\sum_{w\in\mathcal{W}}P_{w}\log P_{w}.

We say that a random variable YY is super-uniform under a probability measure ℍ\mathbb{H} if ℍ⁡(Y≤y)≤y\mathbb{H}(Y\leq y)\leq y for y∈(0,1)y\in(0,1), and it is strictly super-uniform if ℍ⁡(Y≤y)<y\mathbb{H}(Y\leq y)<y for y∈(0,1)y\in(0,1).

Throughout the paper, terms like “increasing” and “decreasing” are in the weak sense, and we follow the convention ∑∅=0\sum_{\varnothing}=0 and ∏∅=1\prod_{\varnothing}=1.

2.2 E-values and e-processes

For a null hypothesis, represented by a set of probabilities (a generic member is denoted by ℙ\mathbb{P}) and a filtration ℱ\mathcal{F}, an e-variable is a nonnegative random variable EE with 𝔼ℙ​[E]≤1\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{P}}[E]\leq 1 (for all ℙ\mathbb{P} in the null hypothesis), and an e-process is a nonnegative stochastic process (Mt)t∈𝕋0(M_{t})_{t\in\mathbb{T}_{0}} adapted to ℱ\mathcal{F} such that 𝔼ℙ​[Mτ]≤1\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{P}}[M_{\tau}]\leq 1 for any stopping time τ\tau with respect to ℱ\mathcal{F}. This means one can monitor evidence continuously without inflating error rates.

For an e-process MM with infinite time horizon, its asymptotic growth rate is defined as the limit

lim infT→∞1T​log⁡MT,\liminf_{T\to\infty}\frac{1}{T}\log M_{T},

under a specific probability measure ℚ\mathbb{Q} in the alternative hypothesis.

Once an e-process MM is constructed, we can sequentially test ℙ\mathbb{P} versus ℚ\mathbb{Q} in the following way: reject the null hypothesis whenever the process MM reaches a threshold 1/α1/\alpha, where α∈(0,1)\alpha\in(0,1) is a pre-specified level. Ville’s inequality (which is equivalent to the optional stopping theorem) gives

ℙ⁡(supt∈𝕋0Mt≥1β)≤β​ for all β>0.\mathbb{P}\left(\sup_{t\in\mathbb{T}_{0}}M_{t}\geq\frac{1}{\beta}\right)\leq\beta\mbox{ for all $\beta>0$}.

Therefore, the type-I error is controlled, even if T=∞T=\infty, and we can use any stopping rule to terminate the process (e.g., stop after 1000 tokens, or stop after seeing MM drop below 0.10.1).

Nonnegative random variables EtE_{t}, t∈𝕋t\in\mathbb{T}, are sequential e-variables if they satisfy 𝔼ℙ​[Et|ℱt−1]≤1\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{P}}[E_{t}|\mathcal{F}_{t-1}]\leq 1 for t∈𝕋t\in\mathbb{T}. An e-process MM is often constructed from the running product of sequential e-variables, that is,

Mt=∏s=1tEs,t∈𝕋0.M_{t}=\prod_{s=1}^{t}E_{s},~~~t\in\mathbb{T}_{0}.

Note that log⁡Mt\log M_{t} is the sum of tt terms log⁡E1,…,log⁡Et\log E_{1},\dots,\log E_{t}, and therefore, intuitively, log⁡Mt\log M_{t} would be large for large tt if the above terms have positive means. Our main task is to construct the e-values (Et)t∈𝕋(E_{t})_{t\in\mathbb{T}} such that the above intuition works rigorously.

The use of e-values and e-processes in the setting of watermark detection naturally analyzes tokens one by one. That is, each e-value EtE_{t} is constructed by one token at step tt, so that they are actually independent. Then, we combine them into an e-process and test the hypothesis via Ville’s inequality as described above. For this reason, in the next section we first focus on the analysis of one token.

3 A mathematical formulation of watermarks

3.1 Watermarks and the detection problem

For now, we focus on just one observation (W,ζ)(W,\zeta), where ζ\zeta is the pseudo-random vector that generates the next token, taking value in a set ZZ, and WW is the token that is chosen. This one-observation setting is simplistic for general testing methods (which typically use the joint data), but it is without loss of generality in constructing e-processes, as we will see later.

The exact distribution of ζ\zeta does not matter, and we can without loss of generality assume that ζ\zeta is uniformly distributed on Z=[0,1]KZ=[0,1]^{K}. Here KK is chosen as the size of the vocabulary 𝒲\mathcal{W}, but again this choice is not important.

An (unbiased) watermarking scheme is a function S:ΔK×Z→[K]S:\Delta_{K}\times Z\to[K] satisfying

ℚ⁡(S⁡(𝐏,ζ)=w)=Pw, for all ​𝐏∈ΔK,w∈𝒲,\displaystyle\mathbb{Q}(S(\mathbf{P},\zeta)=w)=P_{w},~~~\mbox{ for all }\mathbf{P}\in\Delta_{K},~w\in\mathcal{W}, (1)

and ℚ\mathbb{Q} is an objective data generating probability (Li et al., 2025b, ). The condition in (1) can be rewritten as S⁡(𝐏,ζ)∼dCat⁡(𝐏)S(\mathbf{P},\zeta)\mathrel{\mathop{\kern 0.0pt\sim}\limits^{\mathrm{d}}}\mathrm{Cat}(\mathbf{P}) for each 𝐏∈ΔK\mathbf{P}\in\Delta_{K}, where Cat⁡(𝐏)\mathrm{Cat}(\mathbf{P}) is the categorical distribution with probability vector 𝐏\mathbf{P}. There is no other requirement on SS.

For one observed token W∼dCat⁡(𝐏)W\mathrel{\mathop{\kern 0.0pt\sim}\limits^{\mathrm{d}}}\mathrm{Cat}(\mathbf{P}) and ζ\zeta, the null hypothesis H0H_{0} and the alternative hypothesis H1H_{1} are given by

H0:(W,ζ) is independent; H1:W=S⁡(𝐏,ζ).H_{0}:(W,\zeta)\mbox{ is independent; ~~~~ $H_{1}:W=S(\mathbf{P},\zeta)$}.

For a given 𝐏\mathbf{P}, we use 𝕌𝐏\mathbb{U}^{\mathbf{P}} for the distribution of (W,ζ)(W,\zeta) under H0H_{0} and ℚ𝐏\mathbb{Q}^{\mathbf{P}} for the distribution of (W,ζ)(W,\zeta) under H1H_{1}, to emphasize that both 𝕌𝐏\mathbb{U}^{\mathbf{P}} and ℚ𝐏\mathbb{Q}^{\mathbf{P}} depends on the usually unobservable 𝐏\mathbf{P}. This makes the testing problem consisting of composite null and composite alternative. Moreover, ℚ𝐏\mathbb{Q}^{\mathbf{P}} depends on the watermarking scheme SS through the condition (1) on ℚ𝐏\mathbb{Q}^{\mathbf{P}}.

3.2 Constructing general e-values for watermarks

We first analyze how to construct an e-value when we observe one data point (W,ζ)(W,\zeta) to distinguish between H0H_{0} and H1H_{1}. For this problem, an e-variable is a statistic E:𝒲×Z→ℝ+E:\mathcal{W}\times Z\to\mathbb{R}_{+} satisfying the constraint 𝔼ℙ​[E⁡(W,ζ)]≤1\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{P}}[E(W,\zeta)]\leq 1. We write E=E⁡(W,ζ)E=E(W,\zeta) for simplicity.

As well studied in the literature of e-values and explained in Section 2.2, the power of e-variables is usually measured by their expected logarithmic moment. In order to construct a powerful e-value, a standard task is to consider the following optimization problem, for a given 𝐏∈ΔK\mathbf{P}\in\Delta_{K},

maximize\displaystyle\mbox{ maximize } 𝔼ℚ𝐏​[log⁡E]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{Q}^{\mathbf{P}}}[\log E] (2)
over\displaystyle\mbox{ over } statistic ​E≥0; watermarking scheme ​S\displaystyle\mbox{ statistic }E\geq 0;\mbox{ watermarking scheme }S
subject to\displaystyle\mbox{ subject to } 𝔼𝕌𝐑​[E]≤1​ for all 𝐑∈ΔK.\displaystyle\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{U}^{\mathbf{R}}}[E]\leq 1\mbox{ for all $\mathbf{R}\in\Delta_{K}$}.

That is, we optimize the e-power against ℚ𝐏\mathbb{Q}^{\mathbf{P}} for a specific 𝐏\mathbf{P}.

There are two challenges associated with (2), making it impossible to directly solve the optimization problem in practice.

  1. 1.

    The NTP vector 𝐏\mathbf{P} is usually unavailable to the tester in a typical modern LLM.

  2. 2.

    The optimization problem (2) is very complicated, and we are not aware of any methods to solve it, due to the complexity caused by the watermarking scheme SS.

In the next section, we will consider an upper bound for the objective in (2), hoping for a better understanding of the task in the presence of the two challenges. In Section 4, we construct e-values that do not rely on the knowledge of 𝐏\mathbf{P}.

3.3 Static information bounds

A natural upper bound on the e-power in (2) is the Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence of ℚ𝐏\mathbb{Q}^{\mathbf{P}} from 𝕌𝐏\mathbb{U}^{\mathbf{P}}, which measures the difference between the two measures. The KL divergence of a probability measure ℚ1\mathbb{Q}_{1} from another probability ℚ2\mathbb{Q}_{2} is defined as

KL(ℚ1∥ℚ2)\displaystyle\mathrm{KL}(\mathbb{Q}_{1}\|\mathbb{Q}_{2}) =𝔼ℚ1​[log⁡d​ℚ1d​ℚ2]​ if ℚ1≪ℚ2,\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{Q}_{1}}\left[\log\frac{\mathrm{d}\mathbb{Q}_{1}}{\mathrm{d}\mathbb{Q}_{2}}\right]\mbox{~~~ if $\mathbb{Q}_{1}\ll\mathbb{Q}_{2}$,}

and it is ∞\infty otherwise. By Ramdas and Wang, (2025, Theorem 3.20),

𝔼ℚ𝐏[logE]≤KL(ℚ𝐏∥𝕌𝐏)\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{Q}^{\mathbf{P}}}[\log E]\leq\mathrm{KL}(\mathbb{Q}^{\mathbf{P}}\|\mathbb{U}^{\mathbf{P}})

for any e-variable EE, and therefore KL(ℚ𝐏∥𝕌𝐏)\mathrm{KL}(\mathbb{Q}^{\mathbf{P}}\|\mathbb{U}^{\mathbf{P}}) is an upper bound for the e-power in (2). The next proposition gives a simple formula for KL(ℚ𝐏∥𝕌𝐏)\mathrm{KL}(\mathbb{Q}^{\mathbf{P}}\|\mathbb{U}^{\mathbf{P}}).

Proposition 1.

For any watermarking scheme SS and NTP vector 𝐏∈ΔK\mathbf{P}\in\Delta_{K},

KL(ℚ𝐏∥𝕌𝐏)=Ent(𝐏)\mathrm{KL}(\mathbb{Q}^{\mathbf{P}}\|\mathbb{U}^{\mathbf{P}})=\mathrm{Ent}(\mathbf{P})

always holds true. In particular, ℚ𝐏≪𝕌𝐏\mathbb{Q}^{\mathbf{P}}\ll\mathbb{U}^{\mathbf{P}}.

Proof.

Straightforward calculation yields

KL(ℚ𝐏∥𝕌𝐏)\displaystyle\mathrm{KL}(\mathbb{Q}^{\mathbf{P}}\|\mathbb{U}^{\mathbf{P}}) =𝔼ℚ𝐏​[log⁡d​ℚ𝐏d​𝕌𝐏]=∑w∈𝒲Pw​𝔼ℚ𝐏​[log⁡d​ℚ𝐏d​𝕌𝐏∣W=w].\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{Q}^{\mathbf{P}}}\left[\log\frac{\mathrm{d}\mathbb{Q}^{\mathbf{P}}}{\mathrm{d}\mathbb{U}^{\mathbf{P}}}\right]=\sum_{w\in\mathcal{W}}P_{w}\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{Q}^{\mathbf{P}}}\left[\log\frac{\mathrm{d}\mathbb{Q}^{\mathbf{P}}}{\mathrm{d}\mathbb{U}^{\mathbf{P}}}\mid W=w\right].

Note that for any Borel set A⊆ZA\subseteq Z, we have

ℚ𝐏​(ζ∈A∣W=w)\displaystyle\mathbb{Q}^{\mathbf{P}}(\zeta\in A\mid W=w) ≤ℚ𝐏​(ζ∈A)ℚ𝐏​(W=w)\displaystyle\leq\frac{\mathbb{Q}^{\mathbf{P}}(\zeta\in A)}{\mathbb{Q}^{\mathbf{P}}(W=w)}
=𝕌𝐏​(ζ∈A)Pw=𝕌𝐏​(ζ∈A∣W=w)Pw.\displaystyle=\frac{\mathbb{U}^{\mathbf{P}}(\zeta\in A)}{P_{w}}=\frac{\mathbb{U}^{\mathbf{P}}(\zeta\in A\mid W=w)}{P_{w}}. (3)

Thus, d​ℚ𝐏/d​𝕌𝐏≤1/Pw\mathrm{d}\mathbb{Q}^{\mathbf{P}}/\mathrm{d}\mathbb{U}^{\mathbf{P}}\leq 1/P_{w} when W=wW=w, and this implies ℚ𝐏≪𝕌𝐏\mathbb{Q}^{\mathbf{P}}\ll\mathbb{U}^{\mathbf{P}}. It follows that

KL(ℚ𝐏∥𝕌𝐏)\displaystyle\mathrm{KL}(\mathbb{Q}^{\mathbf{P}}\|\mathbb{U}^{\mathbf{P}}) =∑w∈𝒲Pw​𝔼ℚ𝐏​[log⁡d​ℚ𝐏d​𝕌𝐏∣W=w]\displaystyle=\sum_{w\in\mathcal{W}}P_{w}\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{Q}^{\mathbf{P}}}\left[\log\frac{\mathrm{d}\mathbb{Q}^{\mathbf{P}}}{\mathrm{d}\mathbb{U}^{\mathbf{P}}}\mid W=w\right]
≤−∑w∈𝒲PwlogPw=Ent(𝐏).\displaystyle\leq-\sum_{w\in\mathcal{W}}P_{w}\log P_{w}=\mathrm{Ent}(\mathbf{P}).

Therefore, Ent⁡(𝐏)\mathrm{Ent}(\mathbf{P}) is an upper bound on KL(ℚ𝐏∥𝕌𝐏)\mathrm{KL}(\mathbb{Q}^{\mathbf{P}}\|\mathbb{U}^{\mathbf{P}}). To show that the upper bound is attainable, for w∈𝒲w\in\mathcal{W}, let

Aw={z∈Z:S⁡(𝐏,z)=w}.A_{w}=\{z\in Z:S(\mathbf{P},z)=w\}.

Note that (A1,…,AK)(A_{1},\dots,A_{K}) is a partition of ZZ such that

ζ∈Aw⇔W=w.\zeta\in A_{w}\iff W=w.

ℚ𝐏\mathbb{Q}^{\mathbf{P}}-almost surely. This implies

ℚ𝐏​(d​ℚ𝐏d​𝕌𝐏=1Pw∣W=w)=1.\mathbb{Q}^{\mathbf{P}}\left(\frac{\mathrm{d}\mathbb{Q}^{\mathbf{P}}}{\mathrm{d}\mathbb{U}^{\mathbf{P}}}=\frac{1}{P_{w}}\mid W=w\right)=1.

Therefore,

∑w∈𝒲𝔼ℚ𝐏[logd​ℚ𝐏d​𝕌𝐏𝟙{W=w}]=−∑w∈𝒲PwlogPw.\displaystyle\sum_{w\in\mathcal{W}}\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{Q}^{\mathbf{P}}}\left[\log\frac{\mathrm{d}\mathbb{Q}^{\mathbf{P}}}{\mathrm{d}\mathbb{U}^{\mathbf{P}}}\mathds{1}_{\{W=w\}}\right]=-\sum_{w\in\mathcal{W}}P_{w}\log P_{w}.

Hence, the upper bound Ent⁡(𝐏)\mathrm{Ent}(\mathbf{P}) is attained. ∎

By Proposition 1, all watermarking schemes have the same KL(ℚ𝐏∥𝕌𝐏)\mathrm{KL}(\mathbb{Q}^{\mathbf{P}}\|\mathbb{U}^{\mathbf{P}}). This is not surprising, as the joint distribution of (W,ζ)(W,\zeta) is the same for all watermarking schemes, up to a measure-preserving transform on the ZZ space.

In order for

𝔼ℚ𝐏[logE]=KL(ℚ𝐏∥𝕌𝐏),\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{Q}^{\mathbf{P}}}[\log E]=\mathrm{KL}(\mathbb{Q}^{\mathbf{P}}\|\mathbb{U}^{\mathbf{P}}),

it is necessary and sufficient that EE is given by E=d​ℚ𝐏/d​𝕌𝐏E=\mathrm{d}\mathbb{Q}^{\mathbf{P}}/\mathrm{d}\mathbb{U}^{\mathbf{P}} (Ramdas and Wang,, 2025, Theorem 3.20), which depends on the NTP vector 𝐏\mathbf{P}. Moreover, this is usually not a feasible choice of an e-variable, because the constraint in (2),

sup𝐑∈ΔK𝔼𝕌𝐑​[E]≤1,\sup_{\mathbf{R}\in\Delta_{K}}\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{U}^{\mathbf{R}}}[E]\leq 1, (4)

is typically not satisfied, noting that 𝔼𝕌𝐏​[E]=1\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{U}^{\mathbf{P}}}[E]=1, except for the trivial cases where d​ℚ𝐏/d​𝕌𝐏\mathrm{d}\mathbb{Q}^{\mathbf{P}}/\mathrm{d}\mathbb{U}^{\mathbf{P}} does not depend on 𝐏\mathbf{P}.

A strategy to get EE satisfying (4) is to select a pivotal statistic. Fortunately, there is a simple choice that could have nontrivial power: f⁡(UW)f(U_{W}), where (U1,…,UK)=ζ(U_{1},\dots,U_{K})=\zeta is uniformly distributed on Z=[0,1]KZ=[0,1]^{K}, and f:[0,1]→ℝ+f:[0,1]\to\mathbb{R}_{+} is a measurable function. In the next section, we will focus on one of such choices.

3.4 The Gumbel-max watermark

We next describe the Gumbel-max watermark, which is proposed by Aaronson, (2023). As one of the most influential watermark schemes, it has been implemented internally at OpenAI (OpenAI,, 2024) and has become a baseline in many studies (Li et al., 2025b, ; Li et al., 2025c, ). This watermark utilizes the Gumbel-max trick (Gumbel,, 1954; Jang et al.,, 2017) to ensure the unbiasedness characterized in (1). The Gumbel-max watermark operates with the pseudo-random vector ζ=(Uw)w∈𝒲\zeta=(U_{w})_{w\in\mathcal{W}} consisting of iid standard uniform variables, and the decoder is given by

S⁡(𝐏,ζ)=arg​maxw∈𝒲⁡log⁡UwPw.S(\mathbf{P},\zeta)=\argmax_{w\in\mathcal{W}}\frac{\log U_{w}}{P_{w}}. (5)

As suggested by Aaronson, (2023), the pivotal statistic for one token is

Y=UWY=U_{W} (6)

which is uniformly distributed on [0,1][0,1] under the null hypothesis. Therefore, the distribution of YY under 𝕌𝐏\mathbb{U}^{\mathbf{P}} does not depend on 𝐏\mathbf{P}, although the distribution of (W,ζ)(W,\zeta) depends on 𝐏\mathbf{P}. Under the alternative hypothesis ℚ𝐏\mathbb{Q}^{\mathbf{P}}, the distribution of YY depends on 𝐏\mathbf{P}, and it is given by

F𝐏​(y)=ℚ𝐏​(Y≤y)=∑w∈𝒲Pw​y1/Pw​ for y∈[0,1], F^{\mathbf{P}}(y)=\mathbb{Q}^{\mathbf{P}}(Y\leq y)=\sum_{w\in\mathcal{W}}P_{w}y^{1/P_{w}}\mbox{~~~for $y\in[0,1]$, } (7)

with the convention y∞=0y^{\infty}=0 for y<1y<1 and 1∞=11^{\infty}=1. Its density function is

d​F𝐏d​y​(y)=∑w∈𝒲y1/Pw−1,y∈[0,1],\frac{\mathrm{d}F^{\mathbf{P}}}{\mathrm{d}y}(y)=\sum_{w\in\mathcal{W}}y^{1/P_{w}-1},~~~~y\in[0,1], (8)

which is an increasing function of yy. Moreover, it is strictly increasing on [0,1][0,1] unless 𝐏\mathbf{P} is degenerate. As a consequence, YY is strictly super-uniform under the alternative hypothesis for any nondegenerate 𝐏\mathbf{P}, making a test based on YY reasonable.

Putting the subscript tt back to the original detection problem for T<∞T<\infty tokens, we denote by Yt=Ut,WtY_{t}=U_{t,W_{t}} the pivotal statistic for the tt-th token WtW_{t}. Aaronson, (2023) proposed to declare the presence of the watermark if the sum-based statistic Hars=∑t=1Thars​(Yt)H_{\mathrm{ars}}=\sum_{t=1}^{T}h_{\mathrm{ars}}(Y_{t}), with the score function hars​(y)=−log⁡(1−y)h_{\mathrm{ars}}(y)=-\log(1-y), is above a certain threshold. Other score functions, such as the log function hlog​(y)=log⁡yh_{\mathrm{log}}(y)=\log y (Fernandez et al.,, 2023; Kuditipudi et al.,, 2024), and the optimized score function hgum∗h_{\mathrm{gum}}^{*} analyzed in Li et al., 2025b (), can also be adopted in the sum-based approach.

The following lemma gives some properties of F𝐏​(y)F^{\mathbf{P}}(y) as a function of 𝐏\mathbf{P}, which are useful for our later analysis. For two vectors xx and yy in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}, we say that yy majorizes xx, denoted by x≼yx\preccurlyeq y, if ∑i=1kx[i]≤∑i=1ky[i]\sum_{i=1}^{k}x_{[i]}\leq\sum_{i=1}^{k}y_{[i]} for all k∈[n]k\in[n] and ∑i=1nx[i]=∑i=1ny[i]\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_{[i]}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}y_{[i]}, where x[i]x_{[i]} is the ii-th largest component of xx (and analogously for yy). For a set A⊆ℝnA\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n}, a function f:A→ℝf:A\to\mathbb{R} is Schur-convex if

x≼y⟹f⁡(x)≤f⁡(y)x\preccurlyeq y~\Longrightarrow~f(x)\leq f(y)

for x,y∈Ax,y\in A. We refer to Marshall et al., (2011) for a treatment of majorization and Schur-convexity.

Lemma 1.

Let F𝐏F^{\mathbf{P}} be given in (7) and δ∈(0,1/2]\delta\in(0,1/2].

  1. (i)

    For y∈[0,1]y\in[0,1], the function 𝐏→F𝐏​(y)\mathbf{P}\to F^{\mathbf{P}}(y) is Schur-convex on ΔK\Delta_{K}.

  2. (ii)

    For y∈[0,1]y\in[0,1], the vector 𝐏∗=(1−δ,δ,0,…,0)∈ΔKδ\mathbf{P}^{*}=(1-\delta,\delta,0,\dots,0)\in\Delta_{K}^{\delta} maximizes F𝐏​(y)F^{\mathbf{P}}(y) over 𝐏∈ΔKδ\mathbf{P}\in\Delta_{K}^{\delta}.

  3. (iii)

    For any increasing function f:[0,1]→ℝf:[0,1]\to\mathbb{R}, we have

    min𝐏∈ΔKδ⁡𝔼ℚ𝐏​[f⁡(Y)]=𝔼ℚ𝐏∗​[f⁡(Y)].\min_{\mathbf{P}\in\Delta_{K}^{\delta}}\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{Q}^{\mathbf{P}}}[f(Y)]=\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{Q}^{\mathbf{P}^{*}}}[f(Y)].
Proof.

By Proposition C.1 of Marshall et al., (2011), the sum of univariate convex functions is Schur-convex. Therefore, for statement (i), it suffices to prove that p↦p​y1/pp\mapsto py^{1/p} is convex on [0,1][0,1], which follows by straightforward calculus. For statement (ii), it suffices to note that 𝐏≼𝐏∗\mathbf{P}\preccurlyeq\mathbf{P}^{*} for all 𝐏∈ΔKδ\mathbf{P}\in\Delta^{\delta}_{K}, which can be checked by definition. Statement (iii) follows directly from F𝐏​(y)≤F𝐏∗​(y)F^{\mathbf{P}}(y)\leq F^{\mathbf{P}^{*}}(y) for any y∈[0,1]y\in[0,1] and 𝐏∈ΔKδ\mathbf{P}\in\Delta_{K}^{\delta}, as shown in (ii). ∎

Using the Gumbel-max watermark, the maximum e-power for an e-variable is the KL divergence between the two distributions (Theorem 3.20 of Ramdas and Wang,, 2025), that is,

KL(F𝐏∥U)=∑w∈𝒲∫01y1/Pw−1log(∑w∈𝒲y1/Pw−1)dy≤Ent(𝐏),\mathrm{KL}(F^{\mathbf{P}}\|\mathrm{U})=\sum_{w\in\mathcal{W}}\int_{0}^{1}y^{1/P_{w}-1}\log\left(\sum_{w\in\mathcal{W}}y^{1/P_{w}-1}\right)\mathrm{d}y\leq\mathrm{Ent}(\mathbf{P}),

where U\mathrm{U} is the uniform distribution on [0,1][0,1]. Since the mapping from ζ\zeta to YY is not injective, typically KL(F𝐏∥U)<Ent(𝐏)\mathrm{KL}(F^{\mathbf{P}}\|\mathrm{U})<\mathrm{Ent}(\mathbf{P}) holds.

Note that the KL divergence is additive for product measures. Hence, for TT tokens and a constant NTP vector 𝐏\mathbf{P}, the maximum e-power is T×KL(F𝐏∥U)T\times\mathrm{KL}(F^{\mathbf{P}}\|\mathrm{U}). The maximum asymptotic growth rate of any e-process for this watermark is equal to KL(F𝐏∥U).\mathrm{KL}(F^{\mathbf{P}}\|\mathrm{U}).

4 E-processes for watermarks

Throughout this section, we let Yt,t∈𝕋Y_{t},~t\in\mathbb{T} be the pivotal statistics for a watermark scheme. Recall that ℱ=(Ft)t∈𝕋0\mathcal{F}=(F_{t})_{t\in\mathbb{T}_{0}} is the information filtration, to which (Yt)t∈𝕋(Y_{t})_{t\in\mathbb{T}} is adapted, with the interpretation that ℱt−1\mathcal{F}_{t-1} contains all the statistical information available before generating the token wtw_{t}. The sequence (Yt)t∈𝕋(Y_{t})_{t\in\mathbb{T}} satisfies two basic conditions.

Assumption 1.
  1. (i)

    YtY_{t} is uniformly distributed on [0,1][0,1] and independent of ℱt−1\mathcal{F}_{t-1} under the null hypothesis.

  2. (ii)

    YtY_{t} is super-uniform conditional on ℱt−1\mathcal{F}_{t-1} under the alternative hypothesis.

The uniform distribution in Assumption 1 is not essential, because continuously distributed pivotal statistic can be converted to a uniformly distributed one. Condition (ii) does not matter for the validity (type-I error control) of our method, but it affects the power of the method.

In the simple case where ℱt=σ⁡{Y1,…,Yt}\mathcal{F}_{t}=\sigma\{Y_{1},\dots,Y_{t}\} and YtY_{t}, t∈𝕋t\in\mathbb{T} are independent, (i) means that Yt,t∈𝕋Y_{t},~t\in\mathbb{T} are iid uniformly distributed on [0,1][0,1]. The special case of the Gumbel-max watermark is explained in Section 3.4, where Yt=Ut,wtY_{t}=U_{t,w_{t}} for t∈𝕋t\in\mathbb{T} and they satisfy Assumption 1.

4.1 Online test with e-processes

We first introduce (p-to-e) calibrators (Vovk and Wang,, 2021), which convert p-values into e-values. A calibrator is a decreasing function f:[0,1]→ℝ+f:[0,1]\to\mathbb{R}_{+} satisfying ∫01f⁡(p)​𝑑p=1\int_{0}^{1}f(p)\mathrm{d}p=1. Although sometimes only ∫01f⁡(p)​𝑑p≤1\int_{0}^{1}f(p)\mathrm{d}p\leq 1 is required, it is without loss of generality to consider only those with ∫01f⁡(p)​𝑑p=1\int_{0}^{1}f(p)\mathrm{d}p=1.

To use calibrators in an online testing framework, we need random calibrators. For t∈𝕋t\in\mathbb{T}, let Φt\Phi_{t} be the set of all random functions ft:[0,1]→ℝ+f_{t}:[0,1]\to\mathbb{R}_{+} such that

  1. (a)

    ftf_{t} is determined by Y1,…,Yt−1Y_{1},\dots,Y_{t-1} (that is, ftf_{t} is predictable);

  2. (b)

    ftf_{t} is a calibrator for all realizations of Y1,…,Yt−1Y_{1},\dots,Y_{t-1}.

In other words, Φt\Phi_{t} is the set of all predictable calibrators at time tt. We consider the e-process M=(Mt)t∈𝕋0M=(M_{t})_{t\in\mathbb{T}_{0}} defined by

Mt=∏s=1tEs, for ​t∈𝕋0,M_{t}=\prod_{s=1}^{t}E_{s},~~~\mbox{ for }t\in\mathbb{T}_{0}, (9)

where each Et=ft​(1−Yt)E_{t}=f_{t}(1-Y_{t}) for some ft∈Φtf_{t}\in\Phi_{t}. We state the following basic result, which follows from standard arguments in the e-value literature. We present it because it is the most important technical tool for constructing our tests.

Theorem 1.

Under Assumption 1 (i), the process M=(Mt)t∈𝕋0M=(M_{t})_{t\in\mathbb{T}_{0}} in (9) with

Et=ft​(1−Yt),t∈𝕋E_{t}=f_{t}(1-Y_{t}),~~~t\in\mathbb{T}

is an e-process (also a supermartingale), where ft∈Φtf_{t}\in\Phi_{t} for each tt. In particular, under the null hypothesis,

ℙ⁡(supt∈𝕋0Mt≥1/α)≤α​ for all α∈(0,1).\mathbb{P}\left(\sup_{t\in\mathbb{T}_{0}}M_{t}\geq 1/\alpha\right)\leq\alpha~~~\mbox{ for all $\alpha\in(0,1)$.}
Proof.

We first verify that E1,E2,…E_{1},E_{2},\dots are sequential e-values for the null hypothesis. We have

𝔼ℙ​[Et|ℱt−1]=𝔼ℙ​[ft​(1−Yt)|ℱt−1]=∫01ft​(p)​𝑑p≤1,\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{P}}[E_{t}|\mathcal{F}_{t-1}]=\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{P}}[f_{t}(1-Y_{t})|\mathcal{F}_{t-1}]=\int_{0}^{1}f_{t}(p)\mathrm{d}p\leq 1,

where we have used that YtY_{t} is independent of ℱt−1\mathcal{F}_{t-1} and that ftf_{t} is determined by Y1,…,Yt−1Y_{1},\dots,Y_{t-1} and it integrates to at most 11. Moreover, it is clear that EtE_{t} is nonnegative. Therefore,

𝔼ℙ​[Mt|ℱt−1]≤Mt−1,t∈𝕋.\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{P}}[M_{t}|\mathcal{F}_{t-1}]\leq M_{t-1},~~~t\in\mathbb{T}.

Thus, MM is a nonnegative supermartingale starting at 11 and hence an e-process. The last standard statement follows from Ville’s inequality or the optional stopping theorem. ∎

We summarize our online watermark detection procedure in Algorithm 1, where the null hypothesis is rejected as soon as MM reaches 1/α1/\alpha or above. Two parameters T∈ℕ∪{∞}T\in\mathbb{N}\cup\{\infty\} and β∈[0,1)\beta\in[0,1) can be included optionally to terminate the test, declaring no rejection of the null hypothesis. More precisely, the online test stops when TT data points are exhausted or the e-process falls below β\beta. The default values are T=∞T=\infty and β=0\beta=0, meaning that there is no early termination.

In the next two sections, we present two different ways of choosing the calibrator ft∈Φtf_{t}\in\Phi_{t} adaptively.

4.2 Fixed calibrators with adaptive weights

We first consider some fixed choices of deterministic calibrators, which are nonnegative decreasing functions on [0,1][0,1] that integrate to at most 11. Some common examples (Vovk and Wang,, 2021) are, as functions of pp,

2(1−p),p−1/2−1,−logp,and1−p+p​log⁡pp​(log⁡p)2.2(1-p),~~p^{-1/2}-1,~~-\log{p},~~\mbox{and}~~\frac{1-p+p\log{p}}{p(\log{p})^{2}}.

For practical use, we always assume a calibrator gg satisfies ∫01g⁡(p)​𝑑p=1.\int_{0}^{1}g(p)\mathrm{d}p=1.

For a calibrator gg, and t∈𝕋t\in\mathbb{T}, let

Et=(1−λt)+λt​g​(1−Yt),E_{t}=(1-\lambda_{t})+\lambda_{t}g(1-Y_{t}),

where λt\lambda_{t} is [0,1][0,1]-valued and measurable with respect to ℱt−1\mathcal{F}_{t-1}. The e-process M=(Mt)t∈𝕋0M=(M_{t})_{t\in\mathbb{T}_{0}} is then constructed by Mt=∏s=1tEsM_{t}=\prod_{s=1}^{t}E_{s} as in (9). With a given gg, choosing (λt)t∈𝕋(\lambda_{t})_{t\in\mathbb{T}} is a nontrivial task and affects the power of the e-process. A simple choice is to use a pre-specified λ∈(0,1)\lambda\in(0,1), resulting in the process

Mt=∏s=1t(1−λ+λ​g​(1−Ys)),t∈𝕋0.M_{t}=\prod_{s=1}^{t}(1-\lambda+\lambda g(1-Y_{s})),~~~t\in\mathbb{T}_{0}. (10)

We will call the e-process in (10) a nonadaptive e-process.

For better power, (λt)t∈𝕋(\lambda_{t})_{t\in\mathbb{T}} should be chosen adaptively. Using the idea of the empirically adaptive e-process in Ramdas and Wang, (2025, Section 7.8), λt\lambda_{t} is given by λ1=0\lambda_{1}=0 and

λt=arg​maxλ∈[0,γ]⁡{∑s=1t−1log⁡((1−λ)+λ​g​(1−Ys))},t≥2,\lambda_{t}=\argmax_{\lambda\in[0,\gamma]}\left\{\sum_{s=1}^{t-1}\log\left((1-\lambda)+\lambda g(1-Y_{s})\right)\right\},~~~t\geq 2, (11)

where γ∈(0,1]\gamma\in(0,1]. The value of γ\gamma is not important as the maximizer in (11) is typically small except for the first few values of tt, and we will use the typical choice γ=1/2\gamma=1/2 in all implementations. For a calibrator gg and (λt)t∈𝕋(\lambda_{t})_{t\in\mathbb{T}} in (11), we write

f~tg=(1−λt)+λt​g.\tilde{f}^{g}_{t}=(1-\lambda_{t})+\lambda_{t}g. (12)

It is clear that f~tg\tilde{f}^{g}_{t} belongs to Φt\Phi_{t}, and hence Theorem 1 applies to f~tg\tilde{f}^{g}_{t}. The associated e-process is thus

Mt=∏s=1tf~tg(1−Yt),t∈𝕋0,with any nonconstant g and γ∈(0,1),M_{t}=\prod_{s=1}^{t}\tilde{f}^{g}_{t}(1-Y_{t}),~t\in\mathbb{T}_{0},~\mbox{with any nonconstant $g$ and $\gamma\in(0,1)$}, (13)

and we will call it a weight-adaptive e-process.

In our numerical experiments, we find that the calibrator g⁡(p)=−log⁡(p)g(p)=-\log(p) with adaptively chosen λt\lambda_{t} in (11) leads to superior performance over other calibrators or fixed λ\lambda.

4.3 Online Grenander e-processes

Let 𝒟\mathcal{D} be the set of all decreasing density functions on [0,1][0,1] (that is, the set of calibrators). Define the online Grenander (OG) calibrator (Hore et al.,, 2026), by

ftOG=arg​maxf∈𝒟∑s=0t−1logf(1−Ys),t∈𝕋,f^{\mathrm{OG}}_{t}=\argmax_{f\in\mathcal{D}}\sum_{s=0}^{t-1}\log f(1-Y_{s}),~~~t\in\mathbb{T}, (14)

where we set Y0=0Y_{0}=0. The computation of (14) is straightforward as it coincides with the classic Grenander, (1956) estimator applied to (Y0,Y1,…,Yt−1)(Y_{0},Y_{1},\dots,Y_{t-1}): It is known that the unique maximizer in (14) ftOGf^{\mathrm{OG}}_{t}, which is unique on (0,1](0,1] and flexible at 00, is the left derivative of the smallest concave majorant of the empirical distribution function of Y0,Y1,…,Yt−1Y_{0},Y_{1},\dots,Y_{t-1} (see e.g., Chapter 8 of Devroye,, 1987). We say that it is unique because the value of ftOGf_{t}^{\mathrm{OG}} at 00 does not matter, and we can safely set ftOGf_{t}^{\mathrm{OG}} to be continuous at 00. The function ftOGf^{\mathrm{OG}}_{t} is a left-continuous step function. Let

Et=ftOG​(1−Yt),t∈𝕋.E_{t}=f_{t}^{\mathrm{OG}}(1-Y_{t}),~~~\mbox{$t\in\mathbb{T}$.}

Clearly, ftOG∈Φtf_{t}^{\mathrm{OG}}\in\Phi_{t} for each tt.

Note that

f1OG=arg​maxf∈𝒟​log​f​(1),f_{1}^{\mathrm{OG}}=\argmax_{f\in\mathcal{D}}\log f(1),

which is the constant function 11. Therefore, at the first step, the calibrator is chosen as the constant 11, and it evolves as the data Y1,Y2,…Y_{1},Y_{2},\dots are processed. Note that if we remove the term i=0i=0 from (14), then we would have ftOG​(y)=0f_{t}^{\mathrm{OG}}(y)=0 for all y>1−min⁡{Y1,…,Yt−1}y>1-\min\{Y_{1},\dots,Y_{t-1}\}, yielding a positive probability for Et=ftOG​(Yt)=0E_{t}=f_{t}^{\mathrm{OG}}(Y_{t})=0 (which has the same probability as Yt<min⁡{Y1,…,Yt−1}Y_{t}<\min\{Y_{1},\dots,Y_{t-1}\}). This is a situation that we would like to avoid; note that Et=0E_{t}=0 implies Ms=0M_{s}=0 for all s>ts>t. Introducing Y0=0Y_{0}=0 into (14) addresses this issue, but it may be too conservative, as it acts as if the first p-value 1−Y01-Y_{0} is 11. A more lenient choice is

arg​maxf∈𝒟⁡{∑s=1t−1log⁡f⁡(1−Ys)+log⁡f⁡(0)2+log⁡f⁡(1)2},t∈𝕋.\argmax_{f\in\mathcal{D}}\left\{\sum_{s=1}^{t-1}\log f(1-Y_{s})+\frac{\log f(0)}{2}+\frac{\log f(1)}{2}\right\},~~~t\in\mathbb{T}. (15)

Similarly to the case of (14), (15) also yields a constant calibrator 11 at step t=1t=1. Intuitively, (15) uses a Bernoulli distributed Y0Y_{0} with mean 1/21/2, and its computation is the same as the Grenander estimator in (14). The optimizers in each of (14)–(15) belong to Φt\Phi_{t}, and hence Theorem 1 applies to them. We will call the associated e-process

Mt=∏s=1tfsOG(1−Ys),t∈𝕋0, with (fsOG)s∈𝕋0 from (14) or (15)M_{t}=\prod_{s=1}^{t}f_{s}^{\rm OG}(1-Y_{s}),~t\in\mathbb{T}_{0},\mbox{ with $(f^{\rm OG}_{s})_{s\in\mathbb{T}_{0}}$ from \eqref{eq:EA} or \eqref{eq:EA2}} (16)

an OG e-process. Here, for different s,ts,t, we allow fsOGf_{s}^{\rm OG} from (14) and ftOGf_{t}^{\rm OG} from (15), although practically there is no benefit to do so.

Finally, we can include a range [a,b][a,b] with 0<a<1<b<∞0<a<1<b<\infty to the density functions in 𝒟\mathcal{D} in (14)–(15), and we call the resulting e-process in (16) the OG e-process with range [a,b][a,b]. Note ftOGf_{t}^{\rm OG} in (14) has a natural floor ftOG≥1/tf_{t}^{\rm OG}\geq 1/t due to Y0=0Y_{0}=0, which is sufficient for practical purposes. We need the fixed range [a,b][a,b] only for a theoretical result in Section 5.

Remark 1.

A variant of the above construction is that, instead of using all data s=1,…,t−1s=1,\dots,t-1 up to step t−1t-1 to compute ftOGf^{\rm OG}_{t}, we can use a moving window such as s=t−k,…,t−1s=t-k,\dots,t-1 for a fixed kk, which potentially works better for some time-series models. For the problem of LLM watermark detection in this paper, such a variant does not seem to be beneficial. Moreover, instead of a Bernoulli distribution for Y0Y_{0}, we can choose any distribution with mean no larger than 1/21/2 and support including 00, which achieves the same purpose.

In our experiments, we use the formulation in (15), which avoids the issue of being overly conservative and it is computationally efficient.

The OG calibrator is useful in several settings. For instance, Hore et al., (2026) showed that in an iid setting, the OG e-process with range [a,b]⊆(0,∞)[a,b]\subseteq(0,\infty) has an optimal regret bound.

4.4 Average e-processes

Our practical recommendation for constructing the online test is to use the arithmetic average of the OG e-process and the weight-adaptive e-process with the log calibrator g=−logg=-\log. That is, to use

Mt=12​∏s=1tf~sg​(1−Ys)+12​∏s=1tfsOG​(1−Ys),t∈𝕋0.M_{t}=\frac{1}{2}\prod_{s=1}^{t}\tilde{f}^{g}_{s}(1-Y_{s})+\frac{1}{2}\prod_{s=1}^{t}f_{s}^{\rm OG}(1-Y_{s}),~~~t\in\mathbb{T}_{0}. (17)

Clearly, the average of e-processes is an e-process. Alternatively, one can choose different weights than (1/2,1/2)(1/2,1/2) in (17). For simplicity, we will call the e-process in (17) an average e-process.

The test based on the average e-process in (17) may have better performance than both tests based on the individual ones, as shown by our empirical results in Section 6. As a feature of e-processes, the arithmetic average of two e-processes typically has the advantages of the two; see e.g., the mixture e-processes in Ramdas and Wang, (2025). In particular, it is straightforward to see that the asymptotic growth rate of the average e-process is the maximum of those of the two individual e-processes. Taking an average of more than two e-processes (e.g., with different calibrators) also has such a feature, but it does not offer visible further improvements on power performance according to our empirical experiments.

5 Theoretical power guarantees

In practice, the next-token prediction 𝐏t\mathbf{P}_{t} is not available to the tester, and it is not stationary. This makes theoretical power guarantees difficult to analyze. We will first consider a situation that is relevant for the token generating process. Throughout this section, to state asymptotic results, the time horizon is infinite, that is, 𝕋=ℕ\mathbb{T}=\mathbb{N}.

Assumption 2.

For some δ>0\delta>0 and m∈ℕm\in\mathbb{N}, 𝐏t∈ΔKδ\mathbf{P}_{t}\in\Delta^{\delta}_{K} with probability 11 for each tt, and (𝐏t)t∈𝕋(\mathbf{P}_{t})_{t\in\mathbb{T}} is mm-dependent (that is, σ(𝐏t:t≤t1)\sigma(\mathbf{P}_{t}:t\leq t_{1}) and σ(𝐏t:t≥t2)\sigma(\mathbf{P}_{t}:t\geq t_{2}) are independent when t2−t1>mt_{2}-t_{1}>m).

Note that the distribution of (𝐏t)t∈𝕋(\mathbf{P}_{t})_{t\in\mathbb{T}} is the same under both the null and the alternative hypotheses. The assumption δ>0\delta>0 means that the temperature of the LLM is bounded away from 00, and thus the token generating process has enough randomness. The assumption of mm-dependence means that the generation of one token only relies a maximum of mm past tokens. This assumption is needed to apply a form of the law of large numbers. Some other forms of weak or short-term dependence such as α\alpha-mixing are also sufficient for this purpose, and we omit such discussions.

With an e-process MM on an infinite horizon and α∈(0,1)\alpha\in(0,1), we say that the online test at level α\alpha is consistent if

ℚ⁡(sup1≤t≤TMt≥1α)→1​ as T→∞;\mathbb{Q}\left(\sup_{1\leq t\leq T}M_{t}\geq\frac{1}{\alpha}\right)\to 1\mbox{ as $T\to\infty$;}

that is, the probability of rejecting the null hypothesis goes to 11 if the data are generated under the alternative hypothesis. The next result is specific to the Gumbel-max watermarking scheme described in Section 3.4.

Theorem 2.

Suppose that Assumption 2 holds and gg is a nonconstant calibrator. For the Gumbel-max watermark, there exists λ∈(0,1)\lambda\in(0,1) that depends only on δ\delta and gg, such that the nonadaptive e-process MM in (10) has exponential growth under the alternative hypothesis:

lim infT→∞1T​log⁡MT>0​ almost surely.\liminf_{T\to\infty}\frac{1}{T}\log M_{T}>0\mbox{~almost surely.}

In particular, the online test at any level α∈(0,1)\alpha\in(0,1) is consistent.

Proof.

Let Et=g⁡(1−Yt)E_{t}=g(1-Y_{t}) for t∈𝕋t\in\mathbb{T}. The distribution of EtE_{t} depends on 𝐏t\mathbf{P}_{t} through (7), and under ℚ\mathbb{Q} the sequence (log⁡(1−λ+λ​Et)t∈𝕋CLOSE(\log(1-\lambda+\lambda E_{t})_{t\in\mathbb{T}} is mm-dependent. Let λ\lambda be taken as λ0>0\lambda_{0}>0 in Lemma 2 below. Using that lemma, there exists a constant ϵ>0\epsilon>0 such that

𝔼ℚ​[log⁡(1−λ+λ​Et)∣𝐏t]≥ϵ.\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{Q}}[\log(1-\lambda+\lambda E_{t})\mid\mathbf{P}_{t}]\geq\epsilon.

Note that, since d​F𝐏/d​𝕌≤K\mathrm{d}F^{\mathbf{P}}/\mathrm{d}\mathbb{U}\leq K by (8) and YtY_{t} is uniformly distributed under ℙ\mathbb{P}, we have

𝔼ℚ​[(log⁡(1−λ+λ​Et))2∣𝐏t]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{Q}}[(\log(1-\lambda+\lambda E_{t}))^{2}\mid\mathbf{P}_{t}] ≤K​𝔼ℙ​[(log⁡(1−λ+λ​Et))2].\displaystyle\leq K\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{P}}[(\log(1-\lambda+\lambda E_{t}))^{2}].

Since 1−λ+λ​Et1-\lambda+\lambda E_{t}, t∈𝕋t\in\mathbb{T} are identically distributed under ℙ\mathbb{P} with finite mean, 𝔼ℙ​[(log⁡(1−λ+λ​Et))2]\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{P}}[(\log(1-\lambda+\lambda E_{t}))^{2}] is bounded above across tt. Hence, 𝔼ℚ​[(log⁡(1−λ+λ​Et))2]\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{Q}}[(\log(1-\lambda+\lambda E_{t}))^{2}] is also bounded above. This allows us to use the strong law of large numbers for mm-dependent sequences (e.g., Theorem 1 of Hansen,, 1991), which gives

1T​(log⁡MT−𝔼ℚ𝐏​[log⁡MT])→0​ almost surely.\frac{1}{T}\left(\log M_{T}-\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{Q}^{\mathbf{P}}}[\log M_{T}]\right)\to 0\mbox{ almost surely.}

Consequently,

lim infT→∞1T​log⁡MT≥ϵ>0\displaystyle\liminf_{T\to\infty}\frac{1}{T}\log M_{T}\geq\epsilon>0

almost surely, and this proves the desired result. ∎

Lemma 2.

Let YY be the Gumbel-max statistic in (6). For any δ>0\delta>0 and any nonconstant calibrator gg, there exists λ0∈(0,1)\lambda_{0}\in(0,1) such that

inf𝐏∈ΔKδ𝔼ℚ𝐏​[log⁡(1−λ+λ​g​(1−Y))]>0\inf_{\mathbf{P}\in\Delta^{\delta}_{K}}\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{Q}^{\mathbf{P}}}[\log(1-\lambda+\lambda g(1-Y))]>0

for all λ∈(0,λ0]\lambda\in(0,\lambda_{0}].

Proof.

Let UU be uniformly distributed on [0,1][0,1] under ℙ\mathbb{P}. By Lemma 1, For any 𝐏∈ΔKδ\mathbf{P}\in\Delta_{K}^{\delta}, we have

min𝐏∈ΔKδ⁡𝔼ℚ𝐏​[log⁡(1−λ+λ​g​(1−Y))]=𝔼ℚ𝐏∗​[log⁡(1−λ+λ​g​(1−Y))],\displaystyle\min_{\mathbf{P}\in\Delta_{K}^{\delta}}\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{Q}^{\mathbf{P}}}[\log(1-\lambda+\lambda g(1-Y))]=\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{Q}^{\mathbf{P}^{*}}}[\log(1-\lambda+\lambda g(1-Y))], (18)

where 𝐏∗=(1−δ,δ,0,…,0)\mathbf{P}^{*}=(1-\delta,\delta,0,\dots,0). Note that for any 𝐏∈ΔKδ\mathbf{P}\in\Delta^{\delta}_{K},

𝔼ℚ𝐏​[g​(1−Y)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{Q}^{\mathbf{P}}}[g(1-Y)] =𝔼ℙ​[∑w∈𝒲U1/Pw−1​g​(1−U)]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{P}}\left[\sum_{w\in\mathcal{W}}U^{1/P_{w}-1}g(1-U)\right]
>𝔼ℙ​[∑w∈𝒲U1/Pw−1]​𝔼ℙ​[g⁡(1−U)]=1,\displaystyle>\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{P}}\left[\sum_{w\in\mathcal{W}}U^{1/P_{w}-1}\right]\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{P}}\left[g(1-U)\right]=1,

where the inequality follows from Chebyshev’s association inequality, using that gg is nonconstant. This yields, in particular, 𝔼ℚ𝐏∗​[g⁡(1−Y)]>1\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{Q}^{\mathbf{P}^{*}}}[g(1-Y)]>1. By using Theorem 3.14 of Ramdas and Wang, (2025), this further implies

𝔼ℚ𝐏∗​[log⁡(1−λ0+λ0​g​(1−Y))]>0\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{Q}^{\mathbf{P}^{*}}}[\log(1-\lambda_{0}+\lambda_{0}g(1-Y))]>0 (19)

for some λ0>0\lambda_{0}>0. Since the function λ↦log⁡(1−λ+λ​g​(1−Y))\lambda\mapsto\log(1-\lambda+\lambda g(1-Y)) is concave and takes the value 00 at λ=0\lambda=0, we know that it is positive on (0,λ0].(0,\lambda_{0}]. Therefore, using (18), we get the desired statement. ∎

The key property of the Gumbel-max watermark used in Theorem 2 is the uniform bound over ΔKδ\Delta^{\delta}_{K} established in Lemma 1. For given gg and δ\delta, the value of λ\lambda in Theorem 2 can be computed from solving for any λ0>0\lambda_{0}>0 satisfying (19), which is a simple numerical task.

Theorem 2 gives a power-one guarantee for the nonadaptive e-process with a suitably chosen fixed λ∈(0,1)\lambda\in(0,1), which supports using the online test. Nevertheless, the power of the online test for nonadaptive e-process may not be good, because this guarantee needs to guard against all possible NTP vectors, including the most adversarial, but unrealistic, ones. In numerical experiments, we find that the adaptive weights in (12) give rise to much more powerful e-processes.

Next, for a high-level understanding, we consider an idealistic situation. Under this assumption, we can establish the consistency of the weight-adaptive e-process and the OG e-process.

Assumption 3.

The vectors 𝐏1,𝐏2,…\mathbf{P}_{1},\mathbf{P}_{2},\dots are deterministic and identical to 𝐏∈ΔK∘\mathbf{P}\in\Delta_{K}^{\circ}.

Although Assumption 3 is quite unrealistic, it helps to highlight that the weight-adaptive e-process and the OG e-process are reasonable choices, at least in an idealistic setting. The next result is not specific to the Gumbel-max watermark, and applies to all watermark schemes with statistics satisfying the following assumption.

Assumption 4.

Given the constant 𝐏\mathbf{P} in Assumption 3, YtY_{t}, t∈𝕋t\in\mathbb{T} are iid with a strictly super-uniform distribution F𝐏F^{\mathbf{P}} satisfying KL(F𝐏∥U)<∞\mathrm{KL}(F^{\mathbf{P}}\|\mathrm{U})<\infty.

It is straightforward to check that Assumption 4 is satisfied by the Gumbel-max watermark.

Theorem 3.

Suppose that Assumptions 3 and 4 hold. The weight-adaptive e-process MM in (13), the OG e-process MM in (16) with range [a,b][a,b], and the average e-process in (17) all have exponential growth under the alternative hypothesis:

limT→∞1T​log⁡MT>0​ in probability.\lim_{T\to\infty}\frac{1}{T}\log M_{T}>0\mbox{~in probability.}

In particular, the online test at any level α∈(0,1)\alpha\in(0,1) is consistent.

Proof.

First, consider the weight-adaptive e-process MM in (13). For t∈𝕋t\in\mathbb{T}, let Et=g⁡(1−Yt)E_{t}=g(1-Y_{t}). Assumption 1 (ii) guarantees 𝔼ℚ​[Et]>1\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{Q}}[E_{t}]>1. Let

λ∗=arg​maxλ∈[0,γ]⁡𝔼ℚ​[log⁡(1−λ+λ​Et)].\lambda^{*}=\argmax_{\lambda\in[0,\gamma]}\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{Q}}[\log(1-\lambda+\lambda E_{t})].

Note that the optimizer λ∗\lambda^{*} is unique because of the strict concavity of the log function, λ∗\lambda^{*} does not depend on tt because E1,E2,…E_{1},E_{2},\dots are iid, and λ∗>0\lambda^{*}>0, which follows from Theorem 3.14 of Ramdas and Wang, (2025) and the condition 𝔼ℚ​[Et]>1\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{Q}}[E_{t}]>1. Note that

𝔼ℚ​[log⁡(1−λ∗+λ∗​E1)]>0\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{Q}}[\log(1-\lambda^{*}+\lambda^{*}E_{1})]>0 (20)

because λ∗>0\lambda^{*}>0 and it is finite, as guaranteed by Assumption 4. Let

Mt∗=∏s=1t(1−λ∗+λ∗​Es),t∈𝕋0.M^{*}_{t}=\prod_{s=1}^{t}(1-\lambda^{*}+\lambda^{*}E_{s}),~~~t\in\mathbb{T}_{0}.

Proposition EC.2 of Wang et al., (2025) gives

1T​(log⁡MT−log⁡MT∗)=0​ in L1 under ℚ.\frac{1}{T}(\log M_{T}-\log M^{*}_{T})=0\mbox{~~~in $L^{1}$ under $\mathbb{Q}$.}

By the strong law of large numbers,

limT→∞1T​log⁡MT∗=𝔼ℚ​[log⁡(1−λ∗+λ∗​E1)]>0​ almost surely.\lim_{T\to\infty}\frac{1}{T}\log M^{*}_{T}=\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{Q}}[\log(1-\lambda^{*}+\lambda^{*}E_{1})]>0\mbox{~almost surely.}

we get the desired exponential growth of the weight-adaptive e-process.

To show the statement on the OG e-process MM in (16) with range [a,b][a,b], 0<a<1<b<∞0<a<1<b<\infty, we use Theorem 3.1 of Hore et al., (2026), which gives

1T​(log⁡MT−log⁡M~T)=0​ almost surely,\frac{1}{T}(\log M_{T}-\log\widetilde{M}_{T})=0\mbox{~~~almost surely,}

where

M~t=∏s=1tf∗​(1−Yt),t∈𝕋0\widetilde{M}_{t}=\prod_{s=1}^{t}f^{*}(1-Y_{t}),~~~t\in\mathbb{T}_{0}

and f∗f^{*} maximizes 𝔼ℚ​[log⁡f⁡(1−Yt)]\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{Q}}[\log f(1-Y_{t})] over all decreasing densities in 𝒟\mathcal{D} with range [a,b][a,b]. Take any nonconstant calibrator gg that takes values in [a,b][a,b], and let λ∗>0\lambda^{*}>0 be as in the first part of the proof, which satisfies (20). Since 1−λ∗+λ∗​g1-\lambda^{*}+\lambda^{*}g falls in [a,b][a,b], we have

𝔼ℚ​[log⁡f∗​(1−Yt)]≥𝔼ℚ​[log⁡(1−λ∗+λ∗​g​(1−Yt))]>0.\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{Q}}[\log f^{*}(1-Y_{t})]\geq\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{Q}}[\log(1-\lambda^{*}+\lambda^{*}g(1-Y_{t}))]>0.

Therefore, the law of large numbers gives

limT→∞1T​log⁡M~T=𝔼ℚ​[log⁡f∗​(1−Yt)]>0​almost surely.\lim_{T\to\infty}\frac{1}{T}\log\widetilde{M}_{T}=\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{Q}}[\log f^{*}(1-Y_{t})]>0~~~\mbox{almost surely.}

This yields the desired statement on the OG e-process (even stronger, almost sure convergence).

The last statement on the average e-process follows directly from the corresponding statement on the weight-adaptive e-process. ∎

6 Experiments on open-source LLMs

In this section, we investigate the performance of different methods in watermark detection. Specifically, we assess the power of detection procedures based on token sequences generated by simulated or open-source language models with the Gumbel-max watermark (Section 3.4). The comparative analysis includes the following detection methods:

  • •

    The sum-based method using the score function hars​(y)=−log⁡(1−y)h_{\rm ars}(y)=-\log(1-y) (Aaronson,, 2023).

  • •

    The sum-based method using the score function hlog​(y)=log⁡(y)h_{\log}(y)=\log(y) (Fernandez et al.,, 2023; Kuditipudi et al.,, 2024).

  • •

    The optimized sum-based methods using the score function hgum,d∗h_{\text{gum},d}^{*} proposed by Li et al., 2025b (), with the hyper-parameter d=0.1d=0.1 and d=0.01d=0.01, respectively.

  • •

    The weight-adaptive e-process in (13), with the fixed calibrator g⁡(p)=−log⁡(p)g(p)=-\log(p).

  • •

    The OG e-process in (16) with ftOGf^{\rm OG}_{t} calculated by (15).

  • •

    The average e-process in (17) with g⁡(p)=−log⁡(p)g(p)=-\log(p).

We first evaluate these methods on simulated data. The experimental setup essentially follows the approach described in Li et al., 2025b (). We generate a vocabulary 𝒲\mathcal{W} of size 1,000 and assess Type II, Type I and sequential Type I errors throughout 1,000 repeated experiments. Here, sequential Type I errors are computed through sequential monitoring; that is, for t=1,2,…,t=1,2,\dots, we run the test on tt tokens, and declare rejection (watermark is detected) as soon as the test for tt tokens rejects. For traditional tests that are designed for fixed token length, this will inflate the Type I error.

In our simulation, we model LLM’s NTP distributions as spike distributions: we set its largest probability as 1−Δt1-\Delta_{t}, where Δt\Delta_{t} is iid sampled from U⁡(0.001,δ)\mathrm{U}(0.001,\delta) for t=1,⋯,700t=1,\cdots,700 , and the remaining probabilities are firstly sampled from U⁡(0,1)\mathrm{U}(0,1) and subsequently normalized such that ‖𝐏t‖1=1||\mathbf{P}_{t}||_{1}=1. We assess (sequential) Type I error rates on unwatermarked text, and Type II error rates on text generated from the same model with the Gumbel-max watermark. The error rate curves are depicted in Figure 1.

We proceed to investigate the empirical performance of watermark detection methods for text sequences generated by the LLM OPT-1.3B, following the experimental setup in prior works (Kirchenbauer et al.,, 2023; Li et al., 2025b, ). Although OPT-1.3B has fewer parameters compared to commercial LLMs (and it may therefore be regarded as a small language model), evaluating watermark detection methods is a statistical task that is not about the quality or intelligence level of the text generated; we expect similar patterns for the power of watermark detection for more complicated LLMs. The average Type I and Type II error curves are evaluated based on 500 independent repeated experiments.

We present the numerical results under two different temperature parameters (0.5 and 1, respectively) in Figure 2. Together with the simulation results in Figure 1, we have the following findings.

  1. 1.

    Only the e-process methods demonstrate robust Type I error control in both fixed-sample and sequential testing setups. In contrast, the sum-based methods can only provide (asymptotic) Type I error control in the non-sequential setup. In the setting of sequential detection, the Type I error quickly explodes, making these non-e-process methods unsuitable for the online testing task.

  2. 2.

    Some sum-based methods, especially harsh_{\text{ars}}, exhibit better empirical power (one minus Type II error rate) compared to the e-process methods in both the simulated setting and the LLM-generated-text setting. The superior power is expected, as these methods offer weaker statistical validity guarantee.

  3. 3.

    Among the three e-process methods, the OG e-process and the average e-process perform similarly in the simulated setting, visibly better than the weight-adaptive e-process. The weight-adaptive e-process and the average e-process perform similarly in the LLM-generated-text setting, visibly better than the OG e-process. We would therefore recommend the average e-process in practice.

  4. 4.

    The average e-process method has roughly comparable power to the sum-based methods. Perhaps surprisingly, while providing sequential validity, it can even have higher power than the best sum-based methods in some settings of token length and temperature; see the top panel of Figure 2.

  5. 5.

    While Type II error rates for all methods tend to decrease as the text sequences grow longer, sum-based methods exhibit a slight inflation in Type II error rates under low-temperature settings. This inflation in sum-based methods likely stems from the emergence of degenerate NTPs at lower temperatures, particularly in extended sequences—a phenomenon documented in recent studies (Peeperkorn et al.,, 2024; Li et al., 2025a, ). Since tokens generated from degenerate distributions are deterministic and independent of the watermark’s pseudo-randomness, they act as noise that interferes with sum-based detection. In contrast, e-process methods maintain a consistent and monotonic reduction in Type II errors, making them suitable in such situations.

7 Conclusion

In this paper, we presented a unified framework for LLM watermark detection based on e-processes, providing anytime-valid guarantees both theoretically and empirically. Various empirically adaptive e-process construction methods are developed to improve the testing power. In addition, our results analyze the power properties of the proposed procedures, offering insights into their statistical efficiency and asymptotic behavior. Experimental evaluations further demonstrate the advantages of the proposed framework over existing watermark detection methods.

The present study remains preliminary in several aspects. The theoretical characterization of optimal e-process constructions is not yet complete, especially with respect to achieving the upper bounds of e-power. Furthermore, the selection and design of statistically efficient pivotal statistics tailored to different watermark mechanisms warrant deeper investigation. Future work may focus on refining the theoretical limits of sequential testing power within this framework, exploring adaptive and data-driven construction strategies, and developing principled criteria for selecting optimal test statistics under varying watermark schemes. These directions are expected to further strengthen the statistical foundations and practical effectiveness of LLM watermark detection.
